newsitem.title: USA: Probe throws tighter net around former USDA head Espy.
newsitem.headline: Probe throws tighter net around former USDA head Espy.

text.p: A long running government investigation appears to be closing in on former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy, legal experts said Wednesday, after an indictment was returned against Espy's former chief of staff.

Experts agreed that with the indictment of Espy's close aide Ron Blackley on Tuesday -- the first of Espy's former staff to be criminally charged with wrongdoing -- Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz appears to be systematically weaving a tighter net around the former Clinton cabinet member.
"It's fair to say that the investigation is closing in around Mr. Espy," said Georgetown University law professor Paul Rothstein. "Things are looking progressively less good for Mr. Espy."

Espy has been under investigation for 30 months now on charges that while he was Secretary of Agriculture he illegally took gifts and favours from companies and concerns his agency was in charge of regulating.

Smaltz has conducted an aggressive probe that has cost an estimated $9 million and resulted in charges and convictions against a handful of individuals and companies, including major agricultural lobbyists, agribusinesses and a prominent farmer from Espy's home state of Mississippi.

While Rothstein and others noted that the charges brought against Blackley -- making false statements about money he had received while a government employee from individuals with business before the Agriculture Department -- did not mention Espy, they said that applying the pressure to a close associate could help the case against Espy.

"This is an appropriate line of inquiry," said attorney Michael Zeldin. "You look for pressure points in these sort of things, and pressure points are people who surround the target and who know or knew stuff about him."
"In the normal course of an investigation, a prosecutor builds a pyramid ... this is potentially another block in the pyramid," said Zeldin.
Zeldin was deputy independent counsel in a probe that looked into the Bush administration's search into President Bill Clinton's passport files during the 1992 campaign.
But experts said that although the investigation is clearly making progress and is definitely "alive and well," a criminal indictment of Espy is still far from certain.
Rothstein stressed that in many cases the indictment of a senior aide stops at that level if prosecutors cannot prove any wrongdoing by his superior.
"This may be a preliminary step toward indicting the top man, but it may also come up dry ... you cannot tell at this stage," said Rothstein.
An official in Smaltz's office refused to comment on the prospects of indicting the former Agriculture Secretary, but said the investigation of Espy is "still active."

Investigators are also focusing on Arkansas-based poultry processing giant Tyson Foods and its senior chairman Don Tyson, a close friend of Clinton's. Espy allegedly took gifts and favours from Tyson Foods while head of the department, which would be in violation of federal law.
